metadata.title: 1972 Case 41
metadata.original_presentation: A nine-month-old boy was admitted to the hospital because of hepatic enlargement.

required.content: What is the patient's birth and neonatal history?
required.response: The child was the product of a full-term second pregnancy of a 28-year-old mother; gestation was complicated only by iron-deficiency anemia. The birth weight was 15 kg. There was mild neonatal jaundice that cleared on the fourth day.

teaching_points.content: Neonatal jaundice is common and often benign, but persistent or severe cases may indicate underlying conditions such as hemolytic disease.

required.content: What is the family history relevant to the patient's condition?
required.response: There was a family history of hereditary spherocytosis in a five-year-old brother, the mother, the maternal grandfather and a maternal uncle and cousin.

teaching_points.content: Hereditary spherocytosis is an autosomal dominant condition, often presenting with hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly.

required.content: What were the patient's symptoms and medical history leading up to the current admission?
required.response: At the age of two months intermittent icterus developed. The spleen was palpated for the first time, 1 cm below the left costal margin, and the edge of the liver was felt 3 cm below the right costal margin. By the age of six months the liver and spleen were larger. Three weeks before admission wheezing developed and was not responsive to epinephrine; a diagnosis of bronchiolitis was made. One week before admission right otitis media developed and was treated with ampicillin. Bilateral inguinal hernias were noted.

teaching_points.content: Progressive hepatosplenomegaly in infants can be indicative of underlying hematological or metabolic disorders.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Glycogen Storage Disease
additional_information_needed: genetic testing for specific enzyme deficiencies

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Congenital Infection (e.g., CMV, Toxoplasmosis)
refuting_evidence: no specific signs of congenital infection noted

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination upon admission?
required.response: The temperature was 37.7°C, the pulse 105, and the respirations 25. The child was a large, heavy boy who appeared well. Both tympanic membranes were injected, without bulging. There were bilateral expiratory wheezes, with diffuse rhonchi. The heart was normal. The abdomen was markedly distended, and an umbilical hernia was present. The edge of the liver was felt 9 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen 7 cm below the left costal margin. There were bilateral inguinal hernias that descended into the scrotum and could not be reduced.

teaching_points.content: Hepatosplenomegaly and hernias in infants can be associated with systemic conditions such as metabolic or hematological disorders.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hereditary Spherocytosis
supporting_evidence: Intermittent icterus since two months of age
Hepatomegaly and splenomegaly noted on physical exam
additional_information_needed: Peripheral blood smear to look for spherocytes
Complete blood count and reticulocyte count

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Glycogen Storage Disease
refuting_evidence: No mention of hypoglycemia or muscle weakness
Family history more suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis
additional_information_needed: Genetic testing for specific glycogen storage diseases

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency
refuting_evidence: Family history more consistent with hereditary spherocytosis
No mention of liver function abnormalities

required.content: What were the key laboratory findings?
required.response: The hematocrit was 39.9 per cent; the white-cell count was 4300, with 9 per cent neutrophils, 5 per cent band forms, 71 per cent lymphocytes, 7 per cent atypical lymphocytes and 8 per cent monocytes. The reticulocyte count was 2 per cent, and the platelet count 45,000. A blood smear revealed that approximately 5 per cent of the red cells were spherocytes. The prothrombin time was 14.7 seconds, with a control of 12.5 seconds; the partial thromboplastin time was 64.1 seconds. The calcium was 8.4 mg, the phosphorus 3.9 mg, the conjugated bilirubin 1.1 mg, the total bilirubin 1.3 mg, the cholesterol 237 mg, the iron 119 μg, the iron-binding capacity 380 μg, and the protein 4.5 g per 100 ml.

teaching_points.content: Spherocytes on a blood smear are indicative of hereditary spherocytosis, a condition that can lead to hemolytic anemia.

required.content: What were the imaging and biopsy findings?
required.response: An x-ray film of the abdomen confirmed the enlargement of the liver and spleen. A needle-aspiration biopsy of the liver revealed active cirrhosis with regenerative micronodules that were separated by bands of cellular fibrous tissue; excessive hemosiderin was not found.

teaching_points.content: Liver biopsy findings of cirrhosis in infants can indicate chronic liver disease, which may be secondary to metabolic or genetic conditions.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hereditary Spherocytosis
supporting_evidence: Presence of spherocytes on blood smear
refuting_evidence: Liver biopsy showing active cirrhosis, which is not typical for hereditary spherocytosis

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Congenital Hepatic Fibrosis
supporting_evidence: Liver biopsy showing active cirrhosis with regenerative micronodules
refuting_evidence: Family history and presence of spherocytes suggest hereditary spherocytosis
additional_information_needed: Genetic testing for congenital hepatic fibrosis
Assessment for signs of portal hypertension

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Glycogen Storage Disease
refuting_evidence: Liver biopsy did not show excessive glycogen or fat
No hypoglycemia or growth retardation noted
additional_information_needed: Genetic testing for glycogen storage diseases

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Niemann-Pick Disease
refuting_evidence: Liver biopsy did not show excessive lipid storage

required.content: What treatments were administered during the hospital stay?
required.response: Ampicillin, folic acid and phytonadione were administered. A needle-aspiration biopsy of the liver was performed. Bilateral inguinal herniorrhaphy was performed.

teaching_points.content: Management of hereditary spherocytosis often includes folic acid supplementation and may require surgical interventions for complications such as hernias.

required.response: Three weeks after discharge ascites was noted, and chlorothiazide was begun, with a loss of 1 kg in weight. Ten days later, after several days of fever and diarrhea and 18 hours of abdominal discomfort, the child was brought to the hospital. Examination revealed that the abdomen was tender and distended, with absence of bowel sounds. Abdominal paracentesis yielded purulent fluid that contained gram-positive diplococci. Penicillin was given. He died a few hours later.

teaching_points.content: Ascites and abdominal infections in the context of cirrhosis can lead to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, a serious complication requiring prompt treatment.
